diagrams.title: Cloud: Four Models in Two Columns
diagrams.subtitle: Compare each model on the left with its security trait on the right, then reconstruct the sequence.

nodes.label: Public Cloud
nodes.detail: Shared infrastructure provided by a third party. The customer retains data, identities, applications, and configuration: this is shared responsibility.
nodes.exam: Customer misconfiguration (open bucket, overly broad IAM) remains the number one cause of cloud exposure.

nodes.label: Shared Responsibility
nodes.detail: The provider secures the infrastructure; the customer secures everything they place in it, including IAM permissions and serverless functions.
nodes.exam: On the exam, always delineate who owns which layer before proposing a control.

nodes.label: Private Cloud
nodes.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to a single organization, hosted on-premises or by a third party. Stronger control and compliance, but higher cost.
nodes.exam: Private does not mean on-premises: a private cloud can be hosted by an external provider.

nodes.label: Stronger Control
nodes.detail: Isolation facilitates governance and customization, but patching and backup overhead remains with the customer.
nodes.exam: Private cloud does not transfer data responsibility to the provider.

nodes.label: Community Cloud
nodes.detail: Infrastructure shared by multiple organizations with similar requirements (healthcare, finance, research). Peer trust becomes a distinct control.
nodes.exam: Community cloud = trust between organizations in the same consortium, with shared governance.

nodes.label: Peer Trust
nodes.detail: Each peer must define who accesses what and how data is separated, often through a neutral operator.
nodes.exam: In a community scenario, look for data separation and governance, not just encryption.

nodes.label: Hybrid
nodes.detail: Bridge between local environments and the cloud via VPN, dedicated interconnect, and federated identity. This bridge adds a trust boundary.
nodes.exam: In a hybrid scenario, secure the bridge (SSO, VPN, logging on both sides), not just the cloud.

nodes.label: Bridge to Secure
nodes.detail: Traffic crosses an additional boundary: identity federation, encryption in transit, and log correlation.
nodes.exam: Federated SSO (SAML/OIDC) is not just password synchronization.

quiz.question: Which model shares infrastructure among organizations in the same sector?

diagrams.title: IaC, Cloud Resources, and Configuration Drift
diagrams.subtitle: Follow the code to the cloud, then the drift detection and remediation loop.

nodes.label: IaC Repository
nodes.detail: Infrastructure is described in versioned files (Terraform, CloudFormation). Every change goes through code review and a commit.
nodes.exam: IaC turns a network control into a code control: review, signing, and commit history matter.

nodes.label: CI/CD Pipeline
nodes.detail: The pipeline runs the plan, displays differences, and applies changes after approval. This is where policy-as-code is enforced.
nodes.exam: A plan showing an open '0.0.0.0/0' rule must be blocked before apply.

nodes.label: Apply
nodes.detail: The IaC engine creates or modifies resources to match the declared state. Pipeline credentials become service identities to protect.
nodes.exam: An IaC service account with unlimited permissions is a major point of failure.

nodes.label: Cloud Resources
nodes.detail: VMs, buckets, databases, and network rules make up the actual state, which can diverge from the state declared in the repository.
nodes.exam: The source of truth is the versioned code, not the cloud console edited by hand.

nodes.label: Configuration Drift
nodes.detail: A manual change, emergency hotfix, or forgotten script moves the environment away from the expected state: controls are no longer guaranteed.
nodes.exam: Drift is a compliance risk: it reintroduces open ports and access removed in code.

nodes.label: Continuous Detection
nodes.detail: Periodic scans compare the actual state to code and baselines. Detection must also cover resources created outside the pipeline.
nodes.exam: Detecting drift is not enough: it must be correlated with an owner and a timestamp.

nodes.label: Remediation
nodes.detail: Remediate either by reapplying the code or by updating the repository if the manual change was legitimate: code becomes the source of truth again.
nodes.exam: Do not reapply blindly: an emergency fix may be legitimate and must be versioned.

nodes.label: Guardrails as-code
nodes.detail: Automated rules (policy as code) reject non-compliant configurations before deployment: prevention rather than correction.
nodes.exam: Preventive = block before apply; detective = scan after deployment.

quiz.question: Which event creates configuration drift in an IaC environment?

diagrams.title: Cascading Trust Zones
diagrams.subtitle: Traffic flows down from the Internet toward critical assets; each boundary crossing is a control point.

nodes.label: Internet / Untrust
nodes.detail: All traffic here is considered hostile by default: no trust is granted based on source address or network location.
nodes.exam: Untrust = Internet; never allow direct access from this zone to the critical zone.

nodes.label: Firewall / WAF
nodes.detail: The firewall filters ports and addresses; the WAF filters HTTP at the application layer. They enforce policy at the zone boundary.
nodes.exam: WAF = Layer 7; NIPS = inline blocking; NIDS = out-of-band detection.

nodes.label: DMZ
nodes.detail: Buffer zone hosting exposed services (web, SMTP, proxy). A compromised server in the DMZ must not be able to reach the internal network directly.
nodes.exam: DMZ = buffer zone between the Internet (Untrust) and the internal network (Trust).

nodes.label: User Network
nodes.detail: Workstations and internal users: a zone of relative trust, yet a frequent source of phishing and lateral movement.
nodes.exam: 'Trust' is relative: segmentation limits lateral movement between workstations.

nodes.label: NIDS / EDR
nodes.detail: NIDS analyzes a copy of internal traffic; EDR monitors behavior on hosts. They detect what the firewall cannot see.
nodes.exam: An additional trust zone without monitoring becomes a blind spot.

nodes.label: Internal Servers
nodes.detail: Internal applications and databases: access filtered by identity and need-to-know, with centralized logs and OS hardening.
nodes.exam: Apply least privilege between zones, not just from the Internet.

nodes.label: Bastion Host
nodes.detail: Single entry point for administration: MFA, recorded sessions, and temporary access to the critical zone.
nodes.exam: A bastion reduces the administrative surface and provides a centralized audit trail.

nodes.label: Critical Zone
nodes.detail: Most sensitive data and vital systems: named access, encryption, enhanced logging, and no direct path from the Internet.
nodes.exam: The shortest path to critical data must always pass through multiple controls.

quiz.question: Which buffer zone hosts exposed services before the internal network?

diagrams.title: Zero Trust Decision: Identity, Device, Policy, Access
diagrams.subtitle: Never trust, always verify: no access is granted without continuous verification.

nodes.label: User
nodes.detail: A person or service identity requests a resource. Network location is no longer proof of trust.
nodes.exam: Zero Trust verifies BOTH the user AND the device, regardless of the originating network.

nodes.label: Identity + MFA
nodes.detail: The identity provider verifies the account, additional factor, and context (location, time, risk) before issuing a token.
nodes.exam: MFA is the expected control when a password is compromised.

nodes.label: Device Health
nodes.detail: Posture, patches, active antivirus, and encryption are evaluated by the EDR/MDM agent before authorizing the resource.
nodes.exam: An uninventoried personal device must be denied or placed in limited access.

nodes.label: Inventory / MDM
nodes.detail: The decision queries the inventory: is the device registered, does it have an owner, and does it meet compliance policy?
nodes.exam: Without a reliable inventory, Zero Trust policy cannot distinguish a known device from a rogue device.

nodes.label: Adaptive Policy
nodes.detail: Policy combines identity, posture, resource sensitivity, and risk: it defines the authorized access level.
nodes.exam: A policy is 'adaptive' when it accounts for context, not just a user list.

nodes.label: Continuous Decision
nodes.detail: The engine evaluates the request on every access and can revoke a session if context changes: verification is not only at login.
nodes.exam: Zero Trust is continuous: a session valid at the start can be revoked later.

nodes.label: Minimal Access
nodes.detail: Access is limited to the requested resource, at the minimal level and for a fixed duration, with session logging.
nodes.exam: Look for 'least privilege' and 'just-in-time' in exam answers.

nodes.label: Deny / Remediation
nodes.detail: A non-compliant device is denied or isolated; remediation (patching, MDM, inventory) precedes a new attempt.
nodes.exam: Denial must be explicit and logged: silent failures complicate investigation.

quiz.question: Which signal, in addition to identity, is checked before granting access to an internal application?

diagrams.title: Data Lifecycle
diagrams.subtitle: From creation to destruction, each stage triggers its own controls.

nodes.label: Creation
nodes.detail: Data originates from a form, sensor, or process. This is the least expensive moment to decide its classification and minimize collected fields.
nodes.exam: Classify as early as possible: unclassified data triggers no controls.

nodes.label: Classification
nodes.detail: The classification level (public, confidential, sensitive, secret, critical, restricted, top secret) determines encryption, access, retention, and destruction.
nodes.exam: Internal classification and regulatory category (healthcare, finance) are two distinct concepts.

nodes.label: Management / Storage
nodes.detail: Encryption at rest, access control, known location, and backups. Structured and unstructured data are not protected the same way.
nodes.exam: Encryption at rest does not protect against a compromised account reading data in plaintext.

nodes.label: Distribution
nodes.detail: Internal or external sharing: TLS, IPsec, DLP, recipient control, and file labeling to limit spread.
nodes.exam: In transit = channel encryption; DLP monitors content, not just transport.

nodes.label: Retention
nodes.detail: A retention policy sets how long data is kept, based on law, contract, or business need, then triggers archiving.
nodes.exam: Keeping data too long increases the exposure surface: retention is a security control.

nodes.label: Archiving
nodes.detail: Data leaves active use but remains available for audit or legal obligation, with encryption and access control maintained.
nodes.exam: Archiving is not deleting: controls remain active on archives.

nodes.label: Certified Destruction
nodes.detail: Secure erasure, media destruction, or crypto-shredding, with a certificate or proof of erasure. Access revocation accompanies end of life.
nodes.exam: Proof of destruction is required: without a certificate, end of life is not demonstrable.

nodes.label: Continuous Monitoring
nodes.detail: DLP, logging, and access reviews span the entire lifecycle: detecting exfiltration, anomalous access, or data kept past its retention period.
nodes.exam: Controls do not stop at deletion: copies and backups must also be addressed.

quiz.question: At which stage must classification be decided so that controls apply?

diagrams.title: Six Data Roles
diagrams.subtitle: Click a cell to distinguish who decides, who executes, and who verifies quality.

cells.detail: The owner is the business accountable party for the data: they authorize who can read or modify it and choose its sensitivity level.
An admin who applies controls is a custodian: they do not decide who has the right to read HR data.

cells.text: Who is business-accountable for this data?
cells.detail: If no one can answer, classification and authorizations have no credible owner.
Manages backups, encryption, technical permissions, and physical access on behalf of the owner.
The custodian executes the policy defined by the owner; they do not define its purpose.

cells.text: Who operates the system and backups?
cells.detail: Infrastructure, storage, and security teams are typically custodians.
Verifies that data is accurate, well-described, and used in accordance with governance rules.
The custodian ensures technical protection; the steward ensures data quality and meaning.

cells.text: Who ensures the data is accurate and well-described?
cells.detail: Key role for governance, de-identification, and data catalogs.
Enters, corrects, exports, or views data as part of daily work, under the owner's control.
The operator acts within a process defined by others; they do not set the purpose of processing.
Least privilege and action logging apply primarily to this role.
Decides why and how data is processed, often within a legal framework (such as GDPR).
The processor acts on behalf of the controller, according to the contract and its instructions.

cells.text: Why is this data being processed?
cells.detail: The answer identifies the data controller, not the hosting provider.

cells.text: Processes on behalf of the controller
cells.detail: Cloud provider, host, or vendor: executes processing and must comply with the contract and subprocessor rules.
The processor does not act on its own behalf: it remains bound to the controller's instructions.

cells.text: Who processes for us, and under what contract?
cells.detail: Review confidentiality clauses, data residency, and breach notification terms.

diagrams.title: Hot, Warm, Cold Sites: RTO, RPO, and Cost
diagrams.subtitle: Three columns to compare: the faster the recovery, the higher the cost.

nodes.label: Hot Site
nodes.detail: Fully equipped site with continuously or near-continuously synchronized data. Traffic can fail over in minutes.
nodes.exam: Hot site = shortest RTO and highest cost: continuous replication.

nodes.label: RTO minutes · RPO ~0
nodes.detail: Continuous synchronization limits data loss; failover is automated. This is the level required by the most critical services.
nodes.exam: RPO measures data loss; RTO measures service downtime.

nodes.label: Very High Cost
nodes.detail: Two complete environments, replication, and frequent testing: cost is the main limitation of this model.
nodes.exam: An unused hot site must still be tested: an untested recovery is not proven.

nodes.label: Warm Site
nodes.detail: Hardware is installed and configured, but data must be restored from recent backups before services restart.
nodes.exam: Warm site = recovery in hours, a compromise between cost and speed.

nodes.label: RTO hours · RPO hours
nodes.detail: RPO depends on backup frequency; RTO includes restoration time and service validation.
nodes.exam: A 1-hour RPO requires backups or replication at least hourly.

nodes.label: Medium Cost
nodes.detail: You pay for hardware and maintenance, but not full continuous duplication of all production.
nodes.exam: A warm site is often the default choice when RTO is measured in hours.

nodes.label: Cold Site
nodes.detail: Space, power, and connectivity exist, but hardware, software, and data must be shipped and installed before recovery.
nodes.exam: Cold site = recovery in days or weeks, lowest cost.

nodes.label: RTO days · Long RPO
nodes.detail: Shipping and installation time dominate. This model suits low-criticality systems whose outage is acceptable.
nodes.exam: A long RTO is acceptable only if the BCP justifies it for that function.

nodes.label: Low Cost
nodes.detail: Little equipment tied up, but heavy mobilization at the time of the incident and dependence on supply chains.
nodes.exam: Low cost hides a risk: procurement lead time can exceed the stated RTO.

quiz.question: Which site requires restoring data from a backup before restarting services?

diagrams.title: Disaster Recovery Timeline
diagrams.subtitle: T0, RPO, failover, RTO, validation, then failback: put the milestones in order.

nodes.label: Active Backups
nodes.detail: Replication and tested backups before the incident: their frequency determines RPO, and their restorability governs RTO.
nodes.exam: A backup never restored is not a backup: test recovery regularly.

nodes.label: T0 · Incident
nodes.detail: The outage or disaster is detected: the DR plan is activated, stakeholders are notified, and changes are frozen.
nodes.exam: Incident detection and the failover decision are two distinct moments.

nodes.label: RPO · Max Loss
nodes.detail: RPO sets the maximum age of restored data: a 4-hour RPO allows losing up to 4 hours of data.
nodes.exam: RPO = acceptable data loss measured in time, not a restoration deadline.

nodes.label: Failover
nodes.detail: Traffic is redirected to the recovery site: DNS, load balancer, or BGP route. Failover must be documented and tested.
nodes.exam: An unrehearsed manual failover consumes an unpredictable share of the RTO.

nodes.label: RTO · Service Restored
nodes.detail: RTO sets the maximum acceptable service outage duration. It depends on the slowest element in the dependency chain.
nodes.exam: If the network has a 3-hour RTO, email cannot have an effective 1-hour RTO.

nodes.label: Validation
nodes.detail: Verify the integrity of restored data, dependencies, and performance before declaring the service restored to users.
nodes.exam: A service that is 'up' with inconsistent data is not restored.

nodes.label: Failback
nodes.detail: Once the primary site is repaired, data and traffic are moved back under a controlled procedure, often during a maintenance window.
nodes.exam: Failback is a second recovery: it must be planned and tested, not improvised.

nodes.label: Lessons Learned
nodes.detail: Document gaps between target and actual RTO/RPO, then adjust backups, procedures, and exercises.
nodes.exam: Lessons learned feed into the BCP and training: it is a corrective and administrative control.

quiz.question: Which objective sets the maximum acceptable data loss after an incident?

diagrams.title: Control Stack: From Network to Identity
diagrams.subtitle: Five stacked layers: a weak control at one layer is not compensated by a strong control at another.

nodes.label: Identity
nodes.detail: Strong authentication, least privilege, access reviews, and federation: identity is the new perimeter, especially in Zero Trust.
nodes.exam: An over-privileged account bypasses all network controls: identity is a layer in its own right.

nodes.label: Data
nodes.detail: Classification, encryption at rest and in transit, masking, tokenization, and DLP protect data regardless of location.
nodes.exam: DLP acts on sensitive content; encryption acts on readability.

nodes.label: Application
nodes.detail: Input validation, session management, code signing, WAF, and security testing apply controls closest to business logic.
nodes.exam: Validating inputs prevents injection; signing code guarantees origin and integrity.

nodes.label: Host
nodes.detail: Secure baselines, patching, disabling unnecessary services, HIPS/EDR, and device control reduce the attack surface.
nodes.exam: EDR = endpoint agent; XDR = multi-source correlation. Do not confuse either with a firewall.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.detail: Firewalls, NIPS/NIDS, VPNs, 802.1X, and segmentation separate zones and control traffic before it reaches a host.
nodes.exam: IDS is detective; IPS is preventive because it blocks inline.

nodes.label: Firewall / NIPS
nodes.detail: Network and transport layer control: explicit rules, logging of denied traffic, and no direct path to the critical zone.
nodes.exam: A firewall does not protect against a vulnerable application allowed through port 443.

nodes.label: DLP / Masking
nodes.detail: DLP detects and blocks movement of sensitive data; masking limits exposure of fields displayed to users.
nodes.exam: Masking = partially replaced value; tokenization = reversible token via a vault.

nodes.label: MFA / IAM
nodes.detail: MFA, SAML/OIDC federation, and periodic account reviews enforce identity policy on every resource access.
nodes.exam: A forgotten service account is an asset: it belongs in the inventory and access review.

quiz.question: In which layer do encryption, masking, and DLP operate?

diagrams.title: From Detection to Response
diagrams.subtitle: Sensors, SIEM, correlation, alert, triage, and response form an improvement loop.

nodes.label: Sensors / Logs
nodes.detail: System, network, EDR, application, and cloud logs: without synchronized timestamps and complete sources, correlation is impossible.
nodes.exam: NTP and clock synchronization are prerequisites often tested in investigations.

nodes.label: SIEM
nodes.detail: The SIEM aggregates, retains, and indexes events. It applies rules and correlations to surface weak signals.
nodes.exam: SIEM = aggregation and analysis; syslog = simple log transport.

nodes.label: Normalization
nodes.detail: Heterogeneous formats are converted into common fields (user, IP, timestamp) to make events comparable.
nodes.exam: Without normalization, equivalent events remain invisible to correlation rules.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.detail: Cross-referencing multiple events (failed logins then success, then exfiltration) turns noise into a high-confidence signal.
nodes.exam: XDR extends correlation to endpoints, network, and cloud beyond traditional SIEM.

nodes.label: Prioritized Alert
nodes.detail: Alerts are ranked by criticality and asset context: one alert on a critical server outweighs a hundred alerts on a test workstation.
nodes.exam: Too many unprioritized alerts = alert fatigue: prioritization is a control.

nodes.label: SOC Triage
nodes.detail: The analyst verifies whether the alert is real, collects evidence, and decides to escalate, close, or gather more context.
nodes.exam: Triage distinguishes false positive, true positive, and incident: do not escalate everything.

nodes.label: Response
nodes.detail: EDR isolation, session revocation, IP blocking, then eradication and recovery: response follows the incident playbook.
nodes.exam: Contain first, investigate second: the goal is to stop the attack from progressing.

nodes.label: Refined Rules
nodes.detail: Lessons learned tune rules, add sources, and reduce false positives: detection improves after each incident.
nodes.exam: An unmaintained rule becomes noise: tuning is an ongoing activity.

quiz.question: Which step turns multiple isolated events into a high-confidence alert?

diagrams.title: Control Matrix: Type × Category
diagrams.subtitle: Preventive, detective, and corrective crossed with technical, administrative, and physical.

cells.detail: These technical controls prevent the action before it occurs: IPS blocks inline, hardening removes unnecessary services, and encryption renders data unusable without the key.
They reveal anomalous activity without necessarily stopping it: IDS works out-of-band, EDR detects behaviors on the host.
They return the system to a healthy state: EDR isolates the host, quarantine neutralizes a file, and patching fixes the exploited vulnerability.

cells.text: Security policy, training, separation of duties
cells.detail: Written rules and division of responsibilities reduce risk before action: training limits phishing and separation of duties prevents fraud.
Periodic reviews of accounts and logs reveal excessive rights and compliance drift.

cells.text: Incident plan, disciplinary action, procedure update
cells.detail: After a deviation, the incident procedure is followed, policy is corrected, and teams are retrained.
These controls prevent physical access to rooms and media: badges and locks filter entry.
They record or reveal unauthorized presence and provide evidence for investigation.
Physical response consists of interrupting access, confiscating the media, or destroying it per procedure.

diagrams.title: Asset Lifecycle
diagrams.subtitle: Planning, acquisition, assignment, inventory, monitoring, maintenance, then certified decommissioning.

nodes.label: Planning
nodes.detail: Define need, criticality, support duration, native encryption, and certified erasure capability before any purchase.
nodes.exam: Writing security requirements before purchase avoids acquiring unsecurable equipment.

nodes.label: Acquisition
nodes.detail: Purchase, lease, or creation of a cloud resource. Supply chain and vendor origin are part of the evaluation.
nodes.exam: An asset bought without support or update requirements becomes an unpatchable asset.

nodes.label: Assignment
nodes.detail: Name an owner, label the asset, document its authorized use, and record its business criticality.
nodes.exam: Without an owner, no one monitors the asset: assignment creates accountability.

nodes.label: Inventory
nodes.detail: The asset record links identifier, owner, location, version, criticality, data processed, and dependencies: it is a composite inventory.
nodes.exam: A composite inventory links asset, owner, criticality, and dependencies, not just a list of machines.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.detail: Network discovery, MDM, CMDB, and periodic reviews detect ghost assets, shadow IT, and rogue devices.
nodes.exam: A gap between inventory and reality signals a device to investigate, not a simple data-entry error.

nodes.label: Maintenance
nodes.detail: Patching, controlled changes, movement tracking, and status: the asset stays compliant with the baseline throughout its use.
nodes.exam: Patch prioritization depends on the criticality recorded in the inventory.

nodes.label: Decommissioning
nodes.detail: Media erasure or destruction, revocation of access and licenses, then removal from inventory after validation.
nodes.exam: A disk leaving without certified erasure is a potential data breach.

nodes.label: Proof of Destruction
nodes.detail: The certificate of destruction or erasure report attests to the asset's end of life and closes the inventory record.
nodes.exam: Without proof, end of life is not demonstrable during an audit.

quiz.question: Which step creates accountability by naming an owner for the asset?

diagrams.title: Sources of a Composite Inventory
diagrams.subtitle: Five sources converge into a single source of truth, then into remediation.

nodes.label: Active Directory
nodes.detail: Directory: user accounts, service accounts, and computer objects. Links identity to the asset and helps identify owners.
nodes.exam: An orphaned service account is a forgotten asset: it must appear in the inventory.

nodes.label: DHCP
nodes.detail: Leases reveal connected devices, even those not registered in the directory: a very useful passive source for shadow IT.
nodes.exam: DHCP sees a device talking to the network, even if it is not in the directory.

nodes.label: EDR / MDM
nodes.detail: Agents report OS, version, patches, posture, and location: the richest source for asset health.
nodes.exam: Without an agent, a workstation's posture is invisible: EDR and MDM are complementary active sources.

nodes.label: Network Scanner
nodes.detail: Active scans find forgotten hosts, open ports, and unauthorized services that passive sources miss.
nodes.exam: An active scan discovers a ghost server; a poorly calibrated scan can disrupt a sensitive network (OT).

nodes.label: Cloud API
nodes.detail: Provider APIs inventory VMs, buckets, databases, and service identities, including resources created and then forgotten.
nodes.exam: An ephemeral cloud resource may exist for only a few hours: inventory must be near real-time.

nodes.label: Normalization / Dedup
nodes.detail: Merge sources, deduplicate machines (MAC, hostname, cloud ID), and resolve conflicts before feeding the register.
nodes.exam: Without deduplication, the same asset is counted three times and criticality is skewed.

nodes.label: Source of Truth
nodes.detail: The single register holds owner, criticality, versions, data processed, and dependencies: it drives patching, incident response, and recovery.
nodes.exam: A single, up-to-date source of truth is the prerequisite for any remediation prioritization.

nodes.label: Prioritized Action
nodes.detail: The detected gap feeds patching, isolation of a rogue asset, or updating the record: the inventory becomes operational.
nodes.exam: An inventory is useless if it does not trigger action: link it to patching and incident response.

quiz.question: Which active source discovers a forgotten host plugged into the network?
